title: 第171章 天地不公
text:
Grey Sixth told Hua Jiunan none of this — none of the bitterness, none of the old grief. He only thought it quietly to himself: it was all past now. The Little Master had taken pity on their family. Never again would they scavenge like stray dogs, tails between their legs, begging for scraps and getting spat on for their trouble.

For his part, Hua Jiunan had long since made Grey Sixth a brother in his heart, blood in all but name — so he didn't stand on ceremony. He took the manual, flipped through it for a few moments, and had every bit of its fundamentals by heart.

"Sixth Brother, I've got it all. Here's your book back. It'll serve our youngsters well — just the thing to lay their foundations with. Only, the thing's incomplete. If a chance comes, we should hunt down the second half."

Grey Sixth was still sunk deep in memory, and it showed — a heaviness on his face. He took the manual back slowly and tucked it away against his body with careful hands.

Hua Jiunan, reading that heaviness wrong, thought for a moment and then spoke.

"Sixth Brother — the breathing methods, the qi-circulation arts, the Dragon-Tiger binding that I'm passing to you — you can pass them down to our family's sons and grandsons—"

He never finished.

A weight came down on the clearing. On everything. Sudden, vast, invisible — like the whole sky had leaned closer.

Even Zhao Fei, an ordinary man with not one drop of cultivation in him, felt it. He stood there gasping like a landed fish, turning in circles, looking at the others, at the trees, at the ground.

"We was just fine a second ago. The hell is this..."

Chang Baye said nothing at all. He simply coiled — fast, decisive, a big snake folding himself into a tight knot with his head buried in the middle of his own body, and after that he did not move. A stone. A fence post. Furniture that had seen nothing and knew nothing and had no opinions whatsoever.

Chen Daji opened his mouth to crack a joke and Grey Sixth's hand clamped over it.

"You little wretch — one more word and you're a dead one!"

Then, still gripping the boy, he turned back to Hua Jiunan, voice shaking.

"Little Master — the mercy you've shown us, the Grey family will carry it in our hearts forever! But our roots are too shallow. Our stores are too thin. Generations of us, and it all adds up to nothing beside this! We'd never dare dream of handing the Heavenly Master's sacred canon down the generations — please, take back your words!"

That is what he said. But Hua Jiunan was looking at his face, and his face said something else entirely — grief, frustration, a loss so old it had calloused over — and Hua Jiunan saw every bit of it, plain as day.

What does a man live for, in the end? Strip it down, and isn't it just this: to see the people he loves happy?

Something rose in Hua Jiunan like fire up a chimney. He had already guessed what was pressing down on them — and he lifted his head anyway, slow against the weight, and raised three fingers to the night sky.

"Three feet above my head, the gods are watching!"

His voice cracked against the silence, an oath and not a proverb.

"Heaven and Earth, bear witness! Grey Sixth Brother and I are bound by life and death — he has bled for me, again and again, and would bleed again! The old sages said it plain: a man who does not repay kindness is no man at all!"

"So hear me — I offer my own yin-merit, every scrap of grace I've ever stored up, and my allotted lifespan, every year I have left to live! In exchange: three of the Grey family, in every generation, given the right to practice the arts I've passed down!"

Grey Sixth made a sound like a man struck. His knees hit the packed earth — a thud, stone into water — and he kowtowed, full-body, forehead striking the dirt, again, again, again, a terrible mechanical rhythm, dirt on his brow, trying to make himself small enough that heaven would stop punishing the boy who had tried to help him.

"Little Master, your kindness is a sea — the Grey family will remember it generation upon generation, not one second forgotten! But this must not be — please, please take back your words!"

And out of the dark around them, the mice came running.

Out of cracks in the earth, from behind stones, from the shadows at the clearing's edge — dozens of them, a river of small grey bodies pattering across the dirt. They gathered around Hua Jiunan and Grey Sixth, and then, one by one, they stood up on their hind legs. Tiny front paws pressed together at their chests. Whiskers trembling. Black eyes wet, catching what little light there was.

And they bowed. To the empty sky. Again and again, small bodies rocking with the motion, the only sound the whisper of little feet on the earth — the smallest members of the family, begging a silent heaven for mercy.

The pressure kept building.

Zhao Fei went down — flat on his face in the dirt, fingers scraping at the ground, breathing in ragged heaves, pressed toward the earth by something he couldn't see and couldn't name.

Chen Daji didn't understand one bit of what was happening. But he understood this much: somebody was bullying his friends.

And whatever else that fool was, he had never once been short of the courage to die for a friend.

He fought the weight like a man wading through deep water, got his feet under him, thrust one arm straight up, and flipped a single finger at the black sky.

"Goddammit! What is this?! You think you can just push people around?!"

His voice cracked. He didn't care.

"My granny always said — even a killin' ends when the head hits the dirt! Would she lie?! Grey Sixth Brother has kowtowed his heart out to you — what more do you WANT?!"

Still cursing, he hauled Grey Sixth up off the ground by both arms, and the two of them stood together — planted firm, shoulder to shoulder, behind Hua Jiunan.

"Sixth Brother, get up! Begging's no use — then we fight the son of a bitch!"

"To hell with it! Live or die, I'll take it standin' — do your damn worst!"

And then — calm as you please — Chen Daji drew back his fist and punched himself square in the nose. Blood spurted down his lip. He didn't flinch. With the same bleeding hand he dug into his pocket, pulled out a child's slingshot, a Y-shaped stick with a worn rubber band, and aimed it at the infinite sky.

Grey Sixth stood shaking — burned up by the boy's defiance, and by every humiliation of a long lifetime rising in him at once — and then he threw back his head and howled:

"Heaven and Earth are unjust! Fate is unjust! The Grey family will NOT submit!"
